I think the shutdown associated with the COVID pandemic essentially began a chain of events that led to the current rise in inflation. As populations in different areas of the world began having to isolate at home manufacturing began slowing or even stopping in some cases while government authorities tried to figure out how best to respond. Other manufacturers around the world who needed these components to produce their own products were greatly affected. After several months of starting, stopping, and starting again as COVID surges came and went the backlog became critical. Pent up demand for these components/products led to a global supply chain catastrophe at the port authorities as inbound ships couldn't be processed fast enough which led to shortages of products across the country. There weren't enough trains or trucks available to move product across the country and there wasn't enough storage capacity to store all the shipping containers. Meanwhile, domestic oil company production scaled back then stayed flat for over a year. Also, an already relatively tight housing market in the U.S. became even tighter as lumber and other building supply prices rose during this period. As COVID restrictions slowly abated consumer demand rose significantly prompting a rise in prices as product availability was low. The new car market was especially affected as critical chips necessary for cars were backlogged in China. Car dealers couldn't keep new cars on the lots and prices rose for both new cars and used cars. Housing prices reached record highs and gas prices rose significantly as well. This current round of inflation exposed the dependencies of a highly integrated global economy and supply chain and consumers are paying for it now.
